activity.title: 865 endpoints. 800 PRs. 4 weeks. Clayton Winders just published how agents migrated Clipboard's APIs to strict contract validation without disrupting production traffic. These were the endpoints we least wanted to touch: years of partial data migrations, dead experiments, and database internals leaking through. A single "convert this to strict types, make no mistakes" prompt wasn't going to cut it. Neither was a multi-thousand-line PR no one wanted to review. I've written that our thesis is verification over generation. Clayton's post shows what that looks like in practice: 𝗗𝗿𝘆-𝗿𝘂𝗻 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁. A NestJS middleware validates every response against a best-approximation contract and logs mismatches instead of failing requests. There's no better validator than production traffic. 𝗙𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗮𝗹. ~300 endpoints logged contract mismatches despite passing typechecking. Agents triaged the warning logs with an agent skill, encoded the common failure modes, then opened fix PRs. 𝗕𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵 𝗯𝘆 𝗱𝗼𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻. One agent per endpoint produces conflicting changes to shared schemas. One agent for all 865 blows the context window; the contract package alone tokenizes to ~450K tokens. ~40 batches, farmed out by 𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗰𝗿𝗲𝘄 ( https://lnkd.in/geN5-R4h ), hit the sweet spot. 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗼𝘁𝗲 𝗼𝗻 𝗲𝘃𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲. Silence isn't success. An endpoint only graduates from dry-run to strict after serving real traffic with zero warnings. "The agents don't need to be right the first time, they need a way to be told when they're wrong." Full post: https://lnkd.in/gJWwudzz We're hiring engineers who want to build this way: https://lnkd.in/g78Merj4 ...more ...more

The loudest critic of my last post, "with 30 minutes left in my day, I queue tickets, close the lid, and wake up to PRs," said I must be "rubber-stamping slop." He's half right. He's right that no one can meaningfully review 50 substantial pull requests a day. He's wrong about what's in those PRs and underestimates how good agent code gets with the right guardrails. Most tickets aren't features. They're the mundane or forever-backlog work: — Flaky test fixes. Run the candidate fix 50 times in CI; green means it's low-risk to merge. — Dependabot updates that fail CI. Agents triage, fix, or close. — Stale feature flags at 100% rollout. Agents delete the dead branches. — The long tail of a 1M-line JavaScript-to-TypeScript migration. Each one is scoped, with a tight feedback loop where review is cheap. The PR volume is a side effect of clearing that backlog, not a target. What makes it safe to let these run overnight is the harness around the model. I wrote up the rest: How tickets route, what fits, and what doesn't yet. The tools that power it are open-source: https://lnkd.in/gyw3hy2F Thanks to Clayton Winders , who built the initial version. Thanks also to Paul Baranowski , Paulo George Gomes Bezerra , David Huculak , Sarthak Dalabehera, Michael Cook , and Felipe Philipp for early contributions. We're hiring engineers who want to build this: https://lnkd.in/g78Merj4 ...more ...more

You’ve heard of fractional leadership, but have you ever heard of fractional dog ownership? I convinced my sister Priscilla Gray to adopt a dog last year by agreeing that I’d co-own him. Only catch is that she lives so in NC, and I live in CA. She keeps him 99% of the time, I Venmo some money occasionally to help with vet bills and get cute picture of him almost daily and great story if anyone asks, “do you have any pets?” If you’re not REALLY a dog person (🙋🏼‍♀️), it’s the perfect arrangement. Months ago my sister hatched a plan to drive from NC ➡️ CA and decided to bring our dog, Gus, along so he could spend a few days with his other parents. We met up in Yosemite for the prettiest custody exchange you’ve seen and now I guess I’ve got a dog this week?! Please send tips. This is all a long way of saying: watch out for fractional arrangements that seem too good to be true. P.S. if I lose this round of the Clipboard cup to Rocky Warren , its probably the dogs fault… ...more

Can we all agree that we may be holding too low of expectations for the recruiting industry? When I say all, I really mean all - it seems like recruiters, candidates, Talent tech vendors, EVERYONE has just settled for a subpar experience. Let me give you a few recent examples have made me stop and think, "𝘤𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥𝘯'𝘵 𝘸𝘦 𝘢𝘭𝘭 𝘥𝘰 𝘣𝘦𝘵𝘵𝘦𝘳?" ➡️ I was on a call with LinkedIn reviewing some quarterly metrics and was told that that our 21% average InMail acceptance rate was really good and "above industry average". While that's great to hear, in what other world is 21% considered a "good" percentage? ➡️ Our team has been making a concerted effort to give some more specific feedback to candidates, especially when they're rejected at later stages. Hey, you've spent a lot of time with us on a case study and a few live interviews, the least we can do is give a brief summary of why we didn't select you. In ramping this up it has been ASTOUNDING how many candidates reply with some version of, "I'm disappointed, but thank you for the feedback, it's so rare to get any insight on why I was rejected!" I say all of this with an acute awareness that our team at Clipboard has certainly been part of the problem at times, and still has a long way to go. But IMO that doesn't change the fact that if 𝘢𝘴 𝘢𝘯 𝘪𝘯𝘥𝘶𝘴𝘵𝘳𝘺 we're celebrating 21% response rates and viewing a brief bit of feedback after a late stage rejection as a novelty, surely something is just...off? ...more

Our rebrand was - rightly so! - the big news last week, but something else I'm particularly excited about launched along with the rebrand that you may have missed - our new candidate hub. I first got this idea from Adam Horne and Open Org (both must follow's if you work in startup HR/Talent). I saw him post about another startup who had created a public Notion space that does what a really great interview process can do 𝘣𝘦𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘦 someone even applies - give candidates an inside look into how you think, what you value, how you hire, what the dynamics and priorities of each team are, etc. The question I posed to our teams at the start of this project was, "what would a candidate typically ask / learn from us if they were in a live interview with a hiring manager?" We then tried to put as much of that into writing as we possibly could. I love what we have so far, but I'm sure there's still more we could add so would love your help - if you're a candidate considering a job at Clipboard , what else would you like to be able to self-serve in our candidate hub? ...more

Want to know my favorite wellness hack? Talking to strangers. Before you dismiss me as someone who is just hopelessly extroverted, please read the following article that my sister - one of my OG talking to stranger influences - shared the other day: https://lnkd.in/g-fEk5-J . Done? Did you catch the part where there's 𝘲𝘶𝘪𝘵𝘦 𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 a growing body of research that connects saying hi to strangers - or as the author says, building "weak ties" with folks in your day to day life - to increased happiness and improved mental and physical health. And these don't have to be long or in depth conversations - smiling at folks in the street, saying hi to your daily barista, small talking with folks you see on the bus each day - all contribute to these outcomes. Sure, there are times these interactions may be a little awkward, but isn't a moment awkwardness worth a lifetime of increased happiness? So no matter what you may have planned for this spring Sunday, do yourself a favor and say hi to a stranger today. 👋 ...more

activity.title: I can usually tell within the first five minutes whether someone is genuinely ready for a new role, and it often comes down to how they answer two simple questions: “What are you looking for in your next role?” “What’s prompting you to explore a move?” At Clipboard, clarity matters. Ownership matters. How someone thinks matters. The strongest candidates don’t give generic answers. They don’t recite buzzwords or try to guess what I want to hear. And they never speak poorly about a former employer or colleagues. That’s an immediate signal about judgment. Instead, they show intentionality. They talk specifically about the kind of work that energizes them. They describe the environment where they do their best thinking. They’re honest about what’s missing in their role today without negativity. Those early signals matter more than people think. They reveal whether someone is moving toward meaningful ownership, not just away from discomfort. In a high‑growth, high‑autonomy environment, that distinction makes all the difference.

activity.title: Some exciting news: I started Rhema Health with my cofounder Adam Davison and we’re backed by a16z speedrun ! Starting a company in my late 30s meant leaving a wonderful tech career to finally build something of my own. I’ve wanted this since I was a middle schooler building before the web was what it is today, but I needed the right problem to solve. I found it watching my wife’s career in medicine. She poured herself into preventative care for seniors, yet saw how easily proactive work falls through the cracks due to manual tools and administrative overwhelm. Patients were being left behind, and I knew technology could fix that gap. After years of discussions about this problem with friends and at home - it was time. We’re building Rhema. We power preventative care delivery for Medicare providers, improving outcomes for the 70M Americans who depend on it. If you know a healthcare leader serving a Medicare-focused provider group or payer, I’d love to connect. Grateful for the support of Marcus Segal , Joshua Lu , Andrew Chen , Jordan Mazer , Macy Mills , Tom Hammer , Jordan Carver , Andrew Lee , Lester Chen and the rest of the SR team!
